title: One-way functions from errorless average-case NP hardness
formal: Is the following implication true? \[(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\not\subseteq\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{there exists a classical one-way function}.\] Here the antecedent means that some fixed NP language, under some fixed polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble, has no deterministic exact decider with average polynomial running time in the moment sense below. The conclusion asks for a total polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every integer \(c\ge1\), there exists \(n_0\) for which, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\ I}\bigl[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\bigr]\le n^{-c},\qquad z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x)).\] The statement is unrelativized and has no additional hardness, derandomization or cryptographic assumption.
why: A problem can be difficult to decide on typical efficiently generated inputs without obviously providing an efficiently computed map that is hard to invert. Connecting these two kinds of difficulty would clarify the minimum computational assumptions needed for classical cryptography. The precise decision-error and security-length conventions are essential to that comparison.

importance.reason: Whether general average-case computational hardness already provides one-wayness is a foundational gap between complexity theory and cryptography. Resolving this explicit source branch would determine whether useful cryptographic structure follows from broad distributional hardness, rather than requiring specially structured computational assumptions.

sentences: This card selects the average-case-to-one-way-function branch of a broader question in Wigderson’s book.
The hardness assumption concerns exact deterministic decision under an efficiently samplable distribution, with average polynomial time defined by a runtime moment.
The conclusion requires a polynomial-time function that every uniform probabilistic inverter fails to invert with more than negligible probability at all sufficiently large lengths.
Recent heuristic-hardness characterizations, infinitely-often security results and oracle separations use different guarantees.
A resolution would clarify whether broad distributional hardness already forces the computational structure underlying classical one-wayness.

definitions: A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a fixed deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(R\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some \(u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) satisfies \(R(x,u)=1\). A sampler is one probabilistic Turing machine \(S\) that, on the unary size parameter \(1^n\), uses independent unbiased random bits and halts within \(q(n)\) bit steps on every random tape, for a fixed polynomial \(q\). Its exact output distribution is \(D_n\), over finite strings of length at most \(q(n)\). The ensemble parameter \(n\) need not equal the output length. PSamp is the class of these ensembles. A deterministic exact decider \(A\), given \((1^n,x)\), must halt and return the membership bit of \(L\) correctly for every \(n\ge1\) and every finite \(x\), including inputs outside the support of \(D_n\). Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of bit steps. The pair \((L,D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist \(A\), constants \(\alpha>0,C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\alpha]\le C(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). These choices may depend on \(L,S\), but not on \(n\). This is an exact, deterministic moment-based notion, not merely a polynomial first moment or a heuristic allowed to misclassify a small fraction of inputs. The antecedent asserts the existence of one pair \((L,D)\) in the stated class failing this condition. In the conclusion, \(U_n\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings, and the probability also includes the inverter’s independent unbiased coin flips. An inverter is a fixed finite probabilistic Turing program whose running time is polynomial in its input length on every random tape; all reading, writing and arithmetic are charged. It receives both \(1^n\) and \(f(x)\). It may output any preimage of \(f(x)\) of length exactly \(n\), not necessarily the original \(x\); malformed or wrong-length outputs fail. The function \(f\) is computed by one fixed finite deterministic polynomial-time program on all input strings, so output length is automatically polynomially bounded. All programs are uniform and have no advice or oracle. Security is required for all sufficiently large \(n\) for each inverter and exponent; security on only infinitely many lengths is a different guarantee.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must derive the existence of a function with the full uniform, all-sufficiently-large-length inversion guarantee from the stated distributional hardness alone. The implication does not require an efficient black-box transformation from a description of the hard pair. A negative answer must establish the antecedent together with nonexistence of every such function in the unrelativized model; an oracle world, a barrier to one type of reduction or failure of one candidate construction is insufficient. A result assuming randomized heuristic hardness instead of the specified deterministic exact hardness, or yielding only infinitely-often security or a fixed polynomial security gap, does not alone settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.10 groups several implications, from worst-case or average-case hardness to one-way or trapdoor functions. This card selects its average-case-to-one-way branch and spells out the deterministic exact AvgP reading of the book’s distributional discussion. The broader source question is preserved in the import provenance. The worst-case-to-one-way branch is separately represented by TCS-0022; this selection is not claimed equivalent to every branch of the original question.

Bogdanov and Trevisan define strict exact polynomial sampling and the robust moment notion of average running time used here. Randomized heuristics, which may fail or err on a small fraction of inputs, are separate models in that survey and are not silently substituted for this antecedent.

Brzuska and Couteau’s journal paper treats the broad average-case-hardness-to-one-wayness question as unresolved and studies weaker security gaps under stronger hardness notions. Its oracle separations limit types of proof rather than refuting the ordinary unrelativized implication.

Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision gives a characterization involving randomized heuristic hardness and infinitely-often one-way functions. The paper explicitly requires hardness on all sufficiently large instance sizes to upgrade its conclusion to standard security. Its corrected revision changes the approximation regime and does not settle the exact deterministic AvgP implication on this card.

The August 2026 Quantum Pessiland paper constructs oracle worlds with average-case hardness and absent cryptographic primitives. Its theorems are explicitly relative to classical or quantum oracles. Such a separation is relevant evidence about proof limitations, not an unconditional answer to this card.
